title: Imports and Mathematical Context
content: The proof imports Mathlib's matrix and GCD infrastructure. `Mathlib.Data.Matrix.Basic` provides `Matrix.mulVec` and linear operations. `Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.Matrix.IsDiag` gives the diagonal predicate. `Mathlib.Data.Int.GCD` provides `Int.gcdA`, `Int.gcdB`, and `Int.gcd_eq_gcd_ab`. The doc-comment frames this as Open Question OQ-04-OQ-01: generalizing the single-equation parameterization from BezoutIdentityOQ04 to full matrix systems over ℤ.
mathContext: The formalization builds the Smith Normal Form theory for $A \in M_{m \times n}(\mathbb{Z})$, producing a decomposition $A = UDV$ with $U \in \mathrm{GL}_m(\mathbb{Z})$, $V \in \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$, and $D$ diagonal with $d_1 \mid d_2 \mid \cdots \mid d_k$. This structure reduces the system $Ax = b$ to $k$ independent divisibility conditions $d_i \mid (Ub)_i$.

title: Unimodular Matrices: The ℤ-Invertibility Condition
content: A matrix $M \in M_n(\mathbb{Z})$ is **unimodular** iff $\det(M) = \pm 1$. `isUnimodular_iff_abs_det` reformulates this as `Int.natAbs(det M) = 1`, matching the natural number comparison. The proof splits on `Int.natAbs_eq` to handle the positive and negative cases via `omega`. `isUnimodular_one` shows the identity is unimodular (`det_one = 1`). `IsUnimodular.mul` uses `det_mul` and `Int.natAbs_mul` to show the product of unimodulars has `|det| = 1 * 1 = 1`, so the unimodular matrices form a group under multiplication — exactly $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$.
mathContext: By Cramer's rule, $M^{-1} = \det(M)^{-1} \cdot \mathrm{adj}(M)$. For $M^{-1}$ to have integer entries, we need $\det(M)^{-1} \in \mathbb{Z}$, which forces $\det(M) \in \{1, -1\}$ (the units of ℤ). The group $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{Z}) = \{M \in M_n(\mathbb{Z}) : |\det M| = 1\}$ is non-trivial for all $n \geq 1$ and encodes the integer-valued invertibility.

title: Smith Normal Form Structure: Invariant Factors and Decomposition
content: The `SmithNormalForm m n` structure encodes all components of the SNF decomposition: unimodular `U : Matrix (Fin m) (Fin m) ℤ`, diagonal `D : Matrix (Fin m) (Fin n) ℤ`, and unimodular `V : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℤ`. The `hD_diag` field enforces diagonality: all off-diagonal entries are zero. The `hD_div` field encodes the **invariant factor divisibility chain**: $d_k \mid d_{k+1}$ for consecutive diagonal entries, requiring five separate bounds proofs to correctly handle the finite type indexing. `isDecompOf A` simply states $A = U \cdot D \cdot V$.
mathContext: The invariant factors $d_1 \mid d_2 \mid \cdots \mid d_k$ are uniquely determined by $A$ (up to sign): $d_i = \gcd_{i \times i \text{ minors}}(A) / \gcd_{(i-1) \times (i-1) \text{ minors}}(A)$. This uniqueness is what makes SNF a complete invariant for equivalence of integer matrices under unimodular row/column operations. The divisibility chain is NOT present in general diagonal decompositions — it is the distinguishing feature of Smith Normal Form.

title: SNF Existence Axiom: Euclidean Row/Column Reduction
content: The `snf_exists` axiom encodes the fundamental existence theorem: every $m \times n$ integer matrix has a Smith Normal Form. The doc-comment outlines the constructive algorithm: (1) find the smallest $|a_{ij}|$, (2) move to position $(0,0)$ via swaps, (3) use it to clear column 0 and row 0 via Euclidean division, (4) if any remaining entry is not divisible by $d_{11}$, add its row/column to row/column 0 (decreasing $|d_{11}|$), (5) recurse on the lower-right $(m-1) \times (n-1)$ submatrix. Axiomatization is justified by the ~500-line implementation cost.
mathContext: The algorithm terminates because the absolute value of $a_{11}$ strictly decreases in step (4) and $\mathbb{Z}$ is well-ordered under $|\cdot|$. The elementary row operations are left-multiplication by unimodular matrices (transvections, permutation matrices, sign matrices), so $U$ accumulates as their product. Similarly $V$ accumulates column operations. The algorithm runs in $O(mn \cdot \log(\|A\|_\infty))$ steps in practice.

title: Invariant Factor Extraction and Matrix Rank
content: `SmithNormalForm.invariantFactor snf k` extracts the $k$-th diagonal entry $D_{kk}$, returning 0 if $k$ is out of bounds for either dimension. This careful bounds-handling is necessary because `Fin m` and `Fin n` may have different sizes. `SmithNormalForm.rank` counts the number of nonzero diagonal entries using `Finset.filter` and `Finset.card` over `Finset.range (min m n)`. The `noncomputable` annotation is required because this computation involves decidability over integers in a non-constructive setting.
mathContext: The matrix rank of $A$ equals the number of nonzero invariant factors, which equals $\dim_{\mathbb{Q}}(\mathbb{Q}^m \cap \mathrm{colsp}(A))$. For integer matrices, the rank over ℤ and the rank over ℚ coincide. The rank extracted here satisfies $0 \leq r \leq \min(m,n)$ and equals $n - \dim_{\mathbb{Z}}(\ker A)$ by the rank-nullity theorem for free modules.

title: Solvability Criterion: Diagonal Reduction of the System
content: The `snf_solvability_criterion` axiom characterizes solvability of $Ax = b$ via the SNF. Given $A = UDV$, the system becomes $UDV x = b$, i.e., $D(Vx) = Ub$. Setting $y = Vx$ (valid since $V$ is invertible), we get the diagonal system $Dy = Ub$: the $i$-th equation is $d_i y_i = (Ub)_i$. This has a solution iff $d_i \mid (Ub)_i$ (when $d_i \neq 0$) and $(Ub)_i = 0$ (when $d_i = 0$). The axiom captures this reduction without implementing the full SNF machinery.
mathContext: The solvability condition $d_i \mid (Ub)_i$ is equivalent to the system $Ax = b$ having integer solutions. For each $i$: if $d_i \neq 0$, then $y_i = (Ub)_i / d_i \in \mathbb{Z}$ iff $d_i \mid (Ub)_i$; if $d_i = 0$, then $(Ub)_i$ must be 0 (no $y_i$ can make $0 \cdot y_i = c \neq 0$ hold). Once a solution $y$ exists, $x = V^{-1}y$ gives the integer solution (since $V^{-1}$ has integer entries).

title: Classical Bézout Recovery: SNF Specializes to GCD
content: `snf_1x2_invariant_factor` is left as a sorry — connecting the SNF of a $1 \times 2$ matrix $[a, b]$ to $\gcd(a,b)$ requires concrete manipulation of the SNF decomposition. However, `bezout_from_snf` is proved completely **without** using SNF machinery, directly from `Int.gcd_dvd_left/right` and `Int.gcd_eq_gcd_ab`. Forward direction: $\gcd(a,b)$ divides $a$ and $b$, so it divides $ax + by = c$. Backward direction: if $c = k \cdot \gcd(a,b)$, the Bézout coefficients $u = $ `Int.gcdA a b`, $v = $ `Int.gcdB a b` give $x = ku$, $y = kv$.
mathContext: The $1 \times 2$ Smith Normal Form is $[a, b] = [1] \cdot [\gcd(a,b), 0] \cdot V$ where $V = \begin{pmatrix} u & b/d \\ v & -a/d \end{pmatrix}$ with Bézout coefficients $u, v$ and $d = \gcd(a,b)$. The invariant factor is $d_1 = \gcd(a,b)$, confirming that SNF generalizes GCD: 'SNF is GCD for matrices'. The solvability criterion reduces to $\gcd(a,b) \mid c$ — the classical two-variable Bézout criterion.

title: Integer Null Space: A Free ℤ-Submodule
content: `intNullSpace A = {x : Fin n → ℤ | A.mulVec x = 0}` defines the homogeneous kernel. Three theorems establish the ℤ-submodule structure: (1) `zero_mem_intNullSpace` via `mulVec` and `dotProduct` simp lemmas; (2) `intNullSpace_add` via `mulVec_add`: $A(x+y) = Ax + Ay = 0 + 0 = 0$; (3) `intNullSpace_smul` via `mulVec_smul`: $A(kx) = k(Ax) = k \cdot 0 = 0$. Together, these three properties axiomatize a subgroup closed under the ℤ-action — a free ℤ-module of rank $n - r$.
mathContext: The null space $\ker(A) \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^n$ is a free $\mathbb{Z}$-module of rank $n - r$ where $r = $ rank$(A)$. This follows from the structure theorem for finitely generated free modules over PIDs: $\mathbb{Z}^n \cong \ker(A) \oplus \mathrm{im}(A^T)^\perp$, and since $\mathbb{Z}$ is a PID, $\ker(A)$ is itself free. The rank $n - r$ is computed from the null space of the diagonal matrix $D$ in the SNF.

title: Affine Lattice of Solutions: Coset Structure
content: `solution_iff_particular_plus_null` is the key structural theorem: $Ax = b$ iff $x - x_0 \in \ker(A)$. Both directions use `mulVec_sub`: forward, $A(x - x_0) = Ax - Ax_0 = b - b = 0$; backward, $A(x - x_0) = 0$ implies $Ax = Ax_0 = b$. The proof works entirely with `Set.mem_setOf_eq` for the null space membership. The result says the solution set is the **affine lattice** (coset) $x_0 + \ker(A) = \{x_0 + h : h \in \ker(A)\}$.
mathContext: The solution set $\{x \in \mathbb{Z}^n : Ax = b\}$ is a coset of the lattice $\ker(A) \cong \mathbb{Z}^{n-r}$. This generalizes: in 1D ($n = 2, m = 1$), $\ker(A) = \{(bt, -at)\}$ for $t \in \mathbb{Z}$ when $\gcd(a,b) = 1$, recovering the parameterization from BezoutIdentityOQ04. In higher dimensions, the affine lattice has rank $n - r$ and can be visualized as a translate of a hyperplane in $\mathbb{Z}^n$.

title: Concrete Examples: Solvability and Obstruction
content: Three worked examples demonstrate the theory. (1) `three_var_example`: $6x + 10y + 15z = 1$ — since $\gcd(\gcd(6,10), 15) = \gcd(2, 15) = 1$ divides 1, solvable; witness $(1, 1, -1)$ satisfies $6 + 10 - 15 = 1$. (2) `three_var_example_7`: $6x + 10y + 15z = 7$ — same gcd = 1 divides 7; witness $(7, 7, -7)$. (3) `two_var_no_solution`: $6x + 10y = 3$ — $\gcd(6,10) = 2$ does not divide 3; proof shows $2 \mid 6x + 10y = 2(3x+5y)$ but $2 \nmid 3$ via `omega`.
mathContext: These examples illustrate both the positive and negative directions of the solvability criterion. The key insight in (3): $6 = 2 \cdot 3$ and $10 = 2 \cdot 5$, so any linear combination $6x + 10y = 2(3x + 5y)$ is always even. Since $3$ is odd, no solution exists. This is a concrete instance of the general principle: $d \mid ax + by$ for all $x, y$ iff $d \mid a$ and $d \mid b$ (proved as `gcd_divides_linear_combination` in BezoutIdentityOQ04).
